content: The study by Le Gal F, Dziri S, Gerber A, et al. evaluated the performance characteristics of a new commercial kit designed for the quantification of hepatitis D virus (HDV) RNA viral load. This research was published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2017. The study emphasized the importance of immediate laboratory-based reflex testing for individuals who are positive for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) to assess hepatitis D serology. Reflex testing is a systematic approach that can expedite access to HDV treatment and care. HDV and HBV coinfection significantly increase the risk of liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma by twoto three-fold compared to HBV infection alone. Accurate estimates of HDV prevalence and disease burden are essential for developing effective strategies to identify coinfected individuals. Early diagnosis of HDV allows for improved counseling, antiviral therapy, and follow-up care, which can help limit disease progression and transmission. The 2016 Asian-Pacific guidelines and the 2017 European Association for the Study of the Liver guidelines recommend anti-HDV testing for all HBsAg-positive individuals. However, most HBsAg-positive individuals have never been screened for HDV using an anti-HDV assay. Reflex testing for HDV serology can be implemented in two forms: (1) testing for anti-HDV in HBsAg-positive individuals and (2) testing for HDV viremia in anti-HDV-positive individuals. Despite the potential benefits, data on reflex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for HDV viremia are limited. The systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the impact of laboratory-based reflex anti-HDV testing among HBsAg-positive individuals compared to non-reflex approaches. The outcomes assessed included the uptake of HDV antibody and RNA testing, linkage to care, and initiation of treatment. The study followed the Cochrane Handbook guidelines and searched multiple databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Global Health, for studies published before April 2023. Conference proceedings and bibliographic references were also reviewed to minimize publication bias. The analysis included studies that evaluated reflex anti-HDV testing with or without a non-reflex comparator. The outcomes measured were the uptake of HDV antibody and RNA testing, linkage to care, and treatment initiation. There were no restrictions on study design, geographical area, or population. The included studies comprised randomized controlled trials (RCTs), prospective and retrospective cohorts, case-control studies, and data from controlled studies. Non-randomized trials with single-arm designs and uncontrolled longitudinal studies were also included due to limited comparative data. The results showed that reflex testing significantly increased the proportion of HBsAg-positive individuals tested for anti-HDV. For example, 93% of HBsAg-positive cases were assessed for anti-HDV after reflex testing was implemented, compared to only 40% in settings where testing was performed upon clinician request. Reflex testing also improved linkage to care and treatment initiation for HDV-positive individuals. The quality of evidence was rated as very low due to moderate risk of bias and indirectness in the findings. However, reflex testing for HDV serology demonstrated the potential to substantially increase the uptake of HDV antibody testing among HBsAg-positive individuals, facilitating access to HDV treatment and more intensive monitoring. Reflex testing can be integrated into the HBV care cascade, particularly in settings with low HBV prevalence and high HDV prevalence. The study also highlighted the feasibility and cost considerations of scaling up reflex testing. A survey among French microbiologists revealed that 23% of laboratories performed reflex testing for HDV antibody when the first HBsAg-positive test was identified, and 11% performed reflex RNA testing for HDV antibody-positive cases. Reflex testing was perceived as a valuable tool for improving autonomy in conducting anti-HDV and HDV RNA tests. In conclusion, reflex testing for HDV serology is a promising approach to enhance the diagnosis and management of HDV among HBsAg-positive individuals. It can address significant gaps in care and improve outcomes for individuals living with HBV and HDV coinfection. Further research and implementation efforts are needed to optimize reflex testing strategies and integrate them into routine clinical practice.
